newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish court begins pro-Islamist play trial.
newsitem.headline: Turkish court begins pro-Islamist play trial.

text.p: A Turkish court on Wednesday began the trial of 39 people involved in the staging of a pro-Islamist play which allegedly insulted the country's strictly secularist military.
All but five of the defendants were freed pending a final verdict, a defence lawyer told Reuters in the courtroom, crowded with supporters of the defendants.
"Five of the defendants remain in custody, the others are set free," judge Orhan Karadeniz said at the end of the first hearing in Ankara's state security court.
The accused were arrested in April after staging the play, called "An Enemy of God", in the eastern province of Erzurum.
Four actors and the director of the play, who were remanded in custody, face at least 20 years in jail if found guilty. The lawyer said he expected the other defendants to be acquitted.
The play angered the powerful military, which saw it as an attack on the country's secular system.
The generals, who see themselves as the guardians of modern Turkey's secularism, had demanded a government crack down on religious activism in February.
Turkey's first Islamist leader Necmettin Erbakan resigned from the post of prime minister last month under heavy pressure from the armed forces.
In a separate case on Wednesday, a court freed an Islamist former mayor pending a verdict in a trial over an anti-Israel protest which angered the military, witnesses said.
The armed forces sent tanks on to the streets of an Ankara suburb in January following the pro-Islamist evening organised by Sincan district mayor Bekir Yildiz.
Yildiz and five others are on trial for their role in the "Jerusalem night", which enraged secularists who regarded the protest as a call for the implementation of Islamic sharia law.
The mayor, from Erbakan's embattled Islamist Welfare Party, still faces a possible six to 12 years in jail.

Another court found a Moslem preacher linked to Welfare innocent on Wednesday of charges that he "provoked the people to violence on grounds of class, race or religion," state-run Anatolian news agency said.
Ali Kucuker, imam of the mosque at Welfare headquarters in Ankara, had been accused of fostering religious separatism and hatred by preaching against secularism.
